reconcile.note: Keil and Delitzsch treat Ecclesiastes' silence about the dead as an unfinished stage of Old Testament revelation that the New Testament later clarifies and completes.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll quotes Ecclesiastes' beast-like extinction of man against the New Testament's doctrine of everlasting torment as two answers within one canon.

quotes.text: What do you say to the following: "For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no pre-eminence above a beast." … "As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away; so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more."
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Rejoinder to Judge Jeremiah S. Black) (1881), on Ecclesiastes 3:19-20.

sides.snippet: the dead don't know anything, neither do they have any more a reward
sides.verseText: For the living know that they will die, but the dead don't know anything, neither do they have any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.

sides.snippet: The smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever.
sides.verseText: The smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever. They have no rest day and night, those who worship the beast and his image, and whoever receives the mark of his name.
